short: 39-phoneme decoding from dorsal Utah arrays (M06) and overt-speech confound controls (M12) are standard: both have read priors, T5 alone carries them, and folds share words.
position: The paper [@wilson2020decoding] changes two components, and both are standard. The decoder (M06) extends the same group's 10- and 11-class syllable and word decoding from the same participant and arrays [@stavisky2019neural] to 39 phonemes, but the full inventory had already been classified from intracortical [@brumberg2011classification] and ECoG [@mugler2014direct] signals, and the authors' matched test lands at the ECoG level, 36.8% against 36.1% on consonants. The evaluation (M12) adds a contamination test with artifact removal, which none of the 20 prior decoders with full text mentions (Appendix), but the step comes from Roussel et al. [@roussel2020observation], whom the authors credit, other controls preceded it [@anumanchipalli2019speech], and every control runs in T5 alone. The strongest confound is the split: folds are over phoneme instances (Secs. 2.7, 2.8), so the word's other phonemes, whose 500-ms windows overlap the test window, and its other repetitions sit in training; the authors concede that the 420-word dictionary lets windows exploit adjacent phonemes (Sec. 3.2). Their judgment that two dorsal arrays are insufficient for fluent open-vocabulary communication (Sec. 4) holds; "competitive" with ECoG holds only as the ballpark estimate they call it (Sec. 4.1).
